name: EDPB Guidelines 03/2026 on web scraping in the context of generative AI, Version 1.0 (European Data Protection Board, adopted for public consultation 7 July 2026, consultation open until 30 October 2026, final version not expected before end of 2026)
kind: Regulatory guidance document (soft-law interpretive guidance under GDPR, not itself a binding statute but authoritative for how EU/EEA data protection authorities will interpret and enforce GDPR against web-scraping-for-AI-training activity). Currently in DRAFT/consultation status, not final.
maturity: Draft/consultation-stage as of this research pass (published 7 July 2026, consultation closes 30 October 2026, final adoption not expected before end of 2026) -- this project should treat its specifics as PROVISIONAL and subject to change, while treating its general direction (legitimate interest as the near-exclusive viable basis, robots.txt/ai.txt as data-minimization-relevant signals, near-total disfavor of untargeted crawling) as a reliable signal of where enforcement is heading regardless of final wording changes.
license: Not applicable -- this is a legal/regulatory instrument, not licensed software; consulting and citing it is unrestricted, but 'license' as a field does not map onto a regulation (noted per the fields.yaml guidance for non-applicable fields).
keeps_and_discards: Not an extractor. The relevant KEEP/DISCARD distinction the guidelines draw is TARGETED vs. UNTARGETED scraping: targeted scraping (performed against 'more or less restrictive collection criteria,' e.g. specific domains, specific language, specific topic) is treated far more favorably than untargeted crawling ('the software follows each discovered link on an unrestricted basis'), because untargeted collection 'directly undermines demonstrable controller knowledge of holdings' -- the guidelines effectively require an organization to be able to say in advance, and evidence after the fact, WHAT it collected and WHY, which a fully unrestricted crawl cannot satisfy. The practical compliance checklist's item 3 states this explicitly: 'write down your collection criteria before you crawl.'
structure_preserved: Not applicable in the DOM/content-structure sense -- the guidelines are about DATA CATEGORIES and LEGAL BASES, not markup structure. The closest analogue is the requirement (checklist item 6) to 'timestamp data and validate from maintained, official sources' -- a provenance/structural-metadata requirement on the CAPTURED RECORD, not on the captured page's own internal structure.
interactive_elements: Directly relevant via the guidelines' treatment of access-control mechanisms: CAPTCHAs and login walls are explicitly named (alongside robots.txt and ai.txt) as signals the EDPB treats as relevant to both (a) data-minimization expectations and (b) 'reasonable expectations' factors in the Article 6(1)(f) legitimate-interest balancing test -- meaning encountering and RESPECTING a login wall or CAPTCHA (not attempting to bypass it) is itself a compliance-relevant act under this guidance, independent of any technical bot-detection concern.
interactive_state_fidelity: Not addressed -- outside the guidelines' scope, which concerns lawful basis and data categories, not representational fidelity of captured content.
layout_awareness: Not addressed -- the guidelines are agnostic to HOW content is technically captured (layout-aware or not); their concern is WHAT categories of data (personal, special-category) end up retained, regardless of the technical extraction method used to obtain it.
javascript_required: Not addressed directly, though implicitly relevant: since the guidelines require honoring CAPTCHA and login-wall barriers as compliance-relevant signals, a JS-executing browser-based capture tool that could TECHNICALLY bypass such barriers is under the SAME obligation to respect them as a simpler crawler that cannot -- the guidelines do not grant more latitude to more capable tooling, if anything the opposite (capability to bypass raises the bar for demonstrating the bypass was not exploited).
evaluation_method: Not applicable in the empirical-benchmark sense -- this is normative legal guidance, evaluated by legal/regulatory analysis (law firm commentaries, academic critique) rather than by measurement against a corpus. The evidence base for this item is drawn from independent legal commentary (Lexology, ReedSmith, National Law Review/Privacy World, GamingTechLaw) analyzing the EDPB's own published text.
corpus_size_and_origins: Not applicable -- the guidelines are a single regulatory document (EDPB Guidelines 03/2026 v1.0), not a corpus with page/origin counts.
reported_precision_recall: Not applicable -- no precision/recall metric exists for regulatory guidance.
independent_oracle: The single most important structural finding of this item, drawn directly from the Privacy World critique: the EDPB's own guidelines ADMIT there is no true independent oracle for compliance in the AI-training context -- three explicit limitations conceded BY THE EDPB ITSELF: (1) EPISTEMIC -- 'controllers may not know everything they've collected through untargeted crawling,' i.e. the controller cannot even fully audit its own holdings after the fact; (2) TECHNICAL -- 'personal data cannot really be deleted from a trained model' at current technical capacity, meaning an erasure request cannot be VERIFIABLY fulfilled, only approximated via output filtering; (3) INSTITUTIONAL -- 'supervisory authorities lack competence to assess third-party rights questions' at the scale this activity operates at. This triple admission is unusually candid for a regulatory document and directly informs this project's own posture: no external body can currently verify true compliance at the weights level, only at the PROCESS level (documented criteria, honored signals, DPIAs) -- the critique paper's own summary phrase is exact: compliance 'comes closer to a defensible record of diligence than to a demonstrable reduction of interference.'
evidence_independence: The primary source (the EDPB guidelines themselves) is a regulatory body's own output, not vendor-produced, and represents the EU's collective data-protection-authority consensus (EDPB comprises representatives from all EU/EEA national DPAs) -- a genuinely independent, non-commercial source, though clearly a REGULATORY-INTEREST source rather than a neutral technical one. The critique material used in this item (Privacy World/National Law Review, GamingTechLaw) is independent legal-academic/practitioner commentary, not funded by any scraping-tool vendor, giving a reasonably balanced secondary layer.
page_archetype_coverage: Not applicable -- the guidelines classify by DATA CATEGORY (personal data, special-category data under Article 9) and COLLECTION METHOD (targeted vs. untargeted), not by page structural archetype.
script_and_locale_behaviour: Indirectly relevant: 'content written in a specific language' is explicitly named as one example of a valid TARGETING criterion (alongside domain and topic) that would make scraping more defensible under the guidelines -- meaning a language/locale-scoped collection policy is not just a technical nicety for this project but a LEGAL-COMPLIANCE-RELEVANT restriction if EU/EEA data subjects' content might be involved.
leaks_outward: Not the guidelines' framing (they concern lawful COLLECTION and RETENTION, not runtime data leakage to third parties), though the erasure-impossibility problem (see independent_oracle) means that once personal data is absorbed into model weights or a persistent capture store, its effective 'leakage' into any downstream consumer of that model/store becomes UNCONTROLLABLE at the individual-record level -- a structurally similar problem to this project's own concern about what a captured/retained corpus discloses.
mechanism_detectability: Not the guidelines' direct concern (they are about legal basis, not technical stealth), though there IS a structural connection worth naming: this project's own closed_shadow_roots_stay_closed constraint (refusing detectable patching, honestly reporting unreachable content) is philosophically ALIGNED with the guidelines' expectation of honoring robots.txt/CAPTCHA/login-wall signals rather than covertly bypassing them -- both reflect a 'don't defeat access controls, report honestly what was and wasn't accessible' posture, from different motivations (technical honesty vs. legal compliance) arriving at compatible behavior.
countermeasures: Not applicable in the privacy-hardening-technique sense (the guidelines are not a technical countermeasure system); the CLOSEST analogue is the guidelines' own list of 'mitigating measures' which the Privacy World critique treats skeptically: output filters and prompt restrictions, data minimization practices, and source exclusion criteria -- the critique's sharp objection is that 'the data remains in the model's weights; the measures only prevent it from showing,' i.e. these measures mitigate DOWNSTREAM EXPOSURE, not the underlying fact of having retained the data, a distinction this project should keep in mind: filtering OUTPUT is not the same as not having RETAINED input.
measured_fidelity_cost: Not applicable in the technical-fidelity sense; the guidelines' closest analogue is a COMPLIANCE-BURDEN cost, explicitly acknowledged as asymmetric by the GamingTechLaw source: the ten-item practical compliance checklist represents 'genuine engineering requirements, potentially imposing disproportionate burdens on European scale-ups relative to large developers' -- a real cost-asymmetry finding (large incumbents can absorb compliance overhead more easily than smaller operations) directly relevant to any project's own resourcing expectations if it operates at meaningful scale.
gate_state_at_capture: This field is directly, centrally addressed by the guidelines and is one of the most load-bearing findings in this item: robots.txt, ai.txt, CAPTCHAs, and login walls are ALL explicitly named by the EDPB as relevant indicators for (a) data-minimization obligations and (b) the 'reasonable expectations' prong of the Article 6(1)(f) balancing test. The practical compliance checklist directly instructs: 'Honor and log robots.txt, ai.txt, CAPTCHA, and authentication barriers' as item 4 of 10 -- meaning gate state at capture is not merely a metadata nicety for this project, it is a GDPR-relevant compliance signal that should be recorded per capture, matching almost exactly this project's own `gate_state_at_capture` field description ('67% of top sites show a consent interface, so without this a corpus silently mixes gated and ungated captures'). The GamingTechLaw source flags an open question (#2 of 5) about how to handle AMBIGUOUS, POST-COLLECTION, or PLATFORM-IMPOSED (as opposed to site-owner-imposed) versions of these signals -- an unresolved nuance this project should track as the guidelines finalize.
determinism: Not applicable in the technical-system sense -- the guidelines are a legal standard, not a deterministic algorithm; their application involves judgment (the 'balancing test' at the heart of Article 6(1)(f) is explicitly NOT a mechanical/deterministic calculation).
determinism_across_versions: Directly relevant in a different sense: the guidelines are STILL DRAFT (v1.0, consultation-stage), meaning their eventual final text may differ from the version analyzed here -- this project should treat every specific interpretation in this item as subject to revision, and should re-check the final published version before treating any detail as settled.
reproducibility: Not applicable in the technical sense; the guidelines' own TEMPORAL-APPLICATION ambiguity (GamingTechLaw's open question #3: 'whether guidelines apply retroactively to pre-July 2026 datasets or to fine-tuning existing models') is itself a reproducibility-adjacent concern for any organization trying to determine whether PAST collection activity would be judged compliant under a standard that did not yet exist at collection time.
failure_modes: The guidelines' own three self-admitted limitations (epistemic, technical, institutional -- see independent_oracle) ARE the documented failure modes of the regulatory framework itself, an unusually direct self-critique for a regulatory document. Additional failure modes surfaced by the legal commentary: (1) the 'disproportionate effort' exception under Article 14(5)(b) GDPR (which would otherwise excuse an organization from individually notifying every data subject) is narrowly construed by EDPB to cover only archival/research/statistics purposes, EXPLICITLY EXCLUDING commercial model training -- meaning the fallback compliance path becomes a general website notice with a searchable source list, which the critique paper bluntly calls a remedy 'read by no one' in practice; (2) the CJEU GC & Others precedent (originally about search-engine de-indexing of incidentally-collected special-category data) is extended by EDPB to untargeted web crawling, which the GamingTechLaw source calls 'a real analytical leap' -- search engines can de-index individual results, but 'a trained AI model offers nothing comparable,' meaning the legal analogy the EDPB relies on may not actually provide the remedy it implies exists.
failure_visibility: The regulatory framework is, by the critique's own assessment, LOUD about its own limitations (the three admitted gaps are stated plainly, not hidden) but the RESULTING compliance regime is, per the same critique, closer to a paperwork/process standard than a substantive guarantee -- i.e. the guidelines are honest about what they CANNOT enforce, but the compliance mechanisms they DO prescribe (notices nobody reads, output filters that don't remove underlying retention) risk creating an APPEARANCE of resolved failure (a filed DPIA, a published notice) that does not correspond to an actual reduction in the underlying privacy exposure -- a subtle but important distinction between loud ADMISSION and loud REMEDIATION.
scale_limits: Directly relevant to the compliance-burden asymmetry already noted: the ten-item checklist's cost does not scale down proportionally for smaller operators, creating a scale-dependent compliance burden that this project (evidently a smaller/independent operation per its own CLAUDE.md framing) should weigh carefully if any of its captured content could constitute 'personal data' under GDPR and any EU/EEA nexus applies.
delta_cost_model: Not applicable -- no incremental-computation concept in the guidelines.
reanchoring_stability: Not applicable -- no DOM-identity concept in the guidelines.
adversarial_exposure: Not the guidelines' direct framing, though the SPECIAL-CATEGORY data handling section is adjacent: the guidelines extend a search-engine-de-indexing-derived framework to incidentally-collected special-category data (health, political opinion, sexual orientation, etc. under GDPR Article 9), but per the GamingTechLaw critique this creates real risk that INCIDENTAL sensitive-data collection during untargeted crawling 'could be deemed unlawful under Article 9 regardless of applied filters' -- i.e. even a good-faith, non-adversarial capture pipeline can incidentally sweep up legally-sensitive-category data it never specifically sought, and post-hoc filtering may not cure the underlying unlawful COLLECTION even if it prevents downstream EXPOSURE.
provenance_carrying: Directly relevant via checklist item 6: 'timestamp data and validate from maintained, official sources' -- an explicit regulatory endorsement of exactly the kind of per-capture provenance metadata (when captured, from what source) this project's own architecture already prioritizes. Checklist item 7 ('publish Article 14(5)(b) notices with searchable source lists and exclusion rationales') further implies an obligation to maintain, and potentially PUBLISH, a structured record of what was collected and what was deliberately excluded and why -- a provenance requirement extending beyond internal record-keeping into public accountability.
roundtrip_safety: Not applicable -- no serialize/reparse concept in the guidelines.
token_budget_and_ordering: Not applicable -- outside the guidelines' scope.
representation_cost: Not applicable in the token sense, though the checklist's item 5 ('exclude structurally risky sources -- minor-focused sites, sensitive data repositories') is a representation-relevant SCOPING decision this project could adopt as a pre-capture filtering policy independent of any technical representation-efficiency concern.
what_could_be_adopted: Several concrete, directly implementable policy mechanisms, distinct from the technical items elsewhere in this research set: (1) DOCUMENT COLLECTION CRITERIA PROSPECTIVELY, before capture, not retroactively -- directly actionable as a configuration/policy artifact this project could maintain (which domains/languages/topics are in scope, and why) independent of GDPR applicability, simply as good governance hygiene; (2) TREAT robots.txt/ai.txt/CAPTCHA/LOGIN-WALL ENCOUNTERS AS A LOGGED, PER-CAPTURE METADATA FIELD (not just a binary allow/deny gate) -- this maps almost exactly onto this project's own gate_state_at_capture field and should be implemented as a first-class recorded attribute of every capture, exactly as the guidelines require for legal defensibility; (3) PREFER TARGETED OVER UNTARGETED COLLECTION wherever the use case allows it, since the guidelines' entire analytical structure rewards demonstrable, bounded collection scope over unrestricted crawling -- directly reinforcing (from an entirely different, legal-compliance angle) the same discipline a structure-agnostic-but-scope-bounded capture policy would want for its own engineering reasons (predictable ingest cost, auditable corpus composition); (4) EXCLUDE STRUCTURALLY RISKY SOURCE CATEGORIES (minor-focused sites, sensitive-data repositories) as an explicit pre-capture filter, a cheap, high-value precaution regardless of eventual regulatory status.
constraint_violation_ledger: structure_agnosticism: NOT APPLICABLE -- the guidelines concern data CATEGORY and LEGAL BASIS, not page-structure classification; adopting their recommendations introduces no region-naming heuristic and creates no tension with this constraint. no_layout_in_the_fold: NOT APPLICABLE -- same reasoning; the guidelines are layout-agnostic. o_delta: NOT APPLICABLE -- no incremental-computation concept. no_mocks: ADOPTABLE AS-IS AND MEANINGFULLY REINFORCING -- the guidelines' emphasis on honestly logging gate encounters (rather than silently bypassing or silently ignoring them) is philosophically aligned with a no-mocks, no-silent-substitution posture; a system that FAKES having respected a login wall (or silently discards the fact that one was encountered) would violate both the letter of these guidelines and the spirit of no_mocks simultaneously. closed_shadow_roots_stay_closed: NOT DIRECTLY APPLICABLE, BUT ALIGNED IN SPIRIT -- as noted under mechanism_detectability, honoring access-control boundaries rather than covertly defeating them is the same underlying discipline the guidelines require of gate signals (robots.txt/CAPTCHA/login walls) and the project already applies to closed shadow roots; the alignment is thematic, not a direct cross-reference. OVERALL VERDICT: adoptable as-is and directly actionable at the POLICY/GOVERNANCE layer -- this is one of the few items in the entire 17-item batch where the recommended practice (log gate state, document collection criteria, prefer targeted scope) requires essentially no technical reinterpretation to adopt, only a decision to actually implement and maintain the recording discipline the guidelines describe. It imposes NO tension with any of the five hard constraints and REINFORCES two of them (no_mocks, and indirectly the honest-reporting spirit behind closed_shadow_roots_stay_closed).
governance_signal_handling: This field and the guidelines overlap almost completely -- see gate_state_at_capture and what_could_be_adopted above. The one open nuance not yet resolved (GamingTechLaw's open question #2): the guidelines do not yet clarify how to weigh AMBIGUOUS, POST-COLLECTION-MODIFIED, or PLATFORM-IMPOSED-RATHER-THAN-SITE-OWNER-IMPOSED versions of these signals (e.g. a robots.txt that changes after a page was already captured, or an ai.txt imposed by a hosting platform rather than the content's actual publisher) -- this project should track the FINAL version of the guidelines for resolution of this point, and in the meantime should record the SIGNAL STATE AT CAPTURE TIME specifically (a timestamped snapshot, not just a current-state check) to be defensible either way.
legal_basis_and_pii_posture: This field is essentially the guidelines' entire subject; see keeps_and_discards, independent_oracle, and failure_modes above for the substantive content (Article 6(1)(f) legitimate interest as the near-exclusive viable basis with its three-cumulative-condition test: real/lawful/precisely-articulated interest, necessity/no-less-intrusive-alternative, and a balancing test; Article 6(1)(a) consent 'generally not viable... at scale'; Article 9 special-category data 'in principle prohibited absent both an Article 6 basis and an Article 9(2) exception'; 'public visibility is not consent or a legal basis' stated plainly by EDPB). This project, if it retains any content plausibly containing EU/EEA-resident personal data captured via automated means, should treat this document as the current best signal of regulatory expectation even in its draft state.
uncertain: The exact final wording of the three-part Article 6(1)(f) legitimate-interest test AS SPECIFICALLY APPLIED to web scraping (as opposed to the general EDPB Guidelines 1/2024 / Opinion 28/2024 framework it draws from) was not fully extracted verbatim -- only the general three-condition structure (real/lawful/precise interest; necessity; balancing) was confirmed

Whether the guidelines apply retroactively to datasets collected before July 2026, or to fine-tuning of already-trained models, is explicitly UNRESOLVED per the guidelines' own silence on this point (not an extraction gap -- the ambiguity is real and acknowledged by legal commentators as open)
How the guidelines will ultimately interact with the EU AI Act and the 'Digital Omnibus' initiative is explicitly unresolved as of this research pass
Exact retention-period guidance for scraped web content specifically (as distinct from model weights) was not found in available sources and may not yet exist in the guidelines' current draft

This entire item describes a DRAFT, consultation-stage regulatory document (public consultation open until 30 October 2026, final adoption not expected before end of 2026) -- every specific interpretation above should be re-verified against the final published version before being treated as settled compliance guidance
